Reformation

/ref-er-MAY-shun/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Reformation means the process of improving an institution or practice by removing its faults or abuses

Advocates spent a decade pushing for the reformation of the state's overcrowded prison system.

Worked Example

When parents discovered that the district's grading rules punished students for factors beyond their control, they demanded a reformation of the entire policy, and the school board rewrote it from scratch.

The grading policy had clear faults, and the board removed them by rewriting the rules. An organized effort to fix a flawed system is exactly what a reformation is.

How Reformation Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

overhaul

overhaul: a complete repair of a whole system

improvement

improvement: a change that makes something better

restructuring

restructuring: a reorganization of how something works

Antonyms

deterioration

deterioration: a steady worsening

stagnation

stagnation: a failure to change or grow at all

How Strong Is It? — adjustment → reformation → revolution

adjustment vs. reformation

adjustment vs. reformation: An adjustment fixes one small detail, while a reformation repairs the deep faults of an entire system.

revolution vs. reformation

revolution vs. reformation: A reformation improves a system while keeping it standing, but a revolution tears the whole system down and starts over.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-

Prefix — re-: again

Root — form

Root — form: shape

Suffix — -ation

Suffix — -ation: act or process of

Put it together

Put it together: Re- means again, form means shape, and -ation names a process, so a reformation is literally the process of shaping something again, rebuilding a flawed institution into a better one.

Use the root in a new word: transform

Use the root in a new word: transform: A fresh coat of paint can transform a dull room into a cheerful one.

Root Check

Word Choice

Formal / academic

Usually paired with 'of,' as in 'the reformation of the tax code.' With a capital R, the Reformation names a specific sixteenth-century religious movement in Europe, so keep the lowercase general sense separate.
